en: Bowing to Viṣṇu in the form of Narasiṃha, who bears the appearance of hair and whose characteristics are defined by the sequence of the syllables of the Ṛgveda, the wise author sets forth the characteristics of the sequence of the syllables of the Ṛgveda as declared in the ancient scriptures. || 1 ||
Having paid homage to the King of Mantras, the wise Narasiṃha now properly continues the commentary on the sequence of phonemes of the Ṛgvedic verses.

Performing an auspicious invocation, he makes a formal declaration of his intended work with the word *keśa*: “*Keśāḥ*; ‘*kaḥ*’ [Brahmā], ‘*aḥ*’ [Viṣṇu], and ‘*īśaḥ*’ [Rudra]—[the one who bears their forms], Viṣṇu, the Virāṭ Puruṣa. Or rather: ‘From the navel upward is the form of Brahmā; from the throat downward is the body of Viṣṇu; from the hair upward is the form of Rudra; Nṛsiṃha consists of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*).’”
By this statement, the meaning is that one should bow to Narasiṃha; "former treatises" refers to the Śikṣās, Prātiśākhyas, and so forth. || 1 ||
He states the fruit of knowing the sequence of phonemes:
"One who knows the division of the sequence of words, who is expert in the sequence of phonemes, and who knows the distinctions of vowels and measures, may enter the assembly of teachers. (2)

He attains the assembly of teachers; that is, he reaches that divine assembly where Śaunaka and others reside. He is one skilled in the sequence of phonemes; "phonemes" refers to vowels, consonants, and so forth; their "sequence" is their proper order.

In that regard, he is skilled in the knowledge of vowels, consonants, and the combinations consisting of consonant-vowel, vowel-consonant, and consonant-consonant; of the heaviness and lightness of syllables, their equality and doubling, as well as the prohibition of doubling; of *abhinidhāna* (nasalization) and the prohibition of *abhinidhāna*; of augmentations (*āgama*), whether natural (*prākṛta*) or modified (*vaikṛta*); of vowels with nasals (*sānunāsika*) and without nasals (*niranunāsika*); of the *yama* sounds, the *svarabhakti*, and so forth; of phonemes, nasalization (*anusvāra*), the visarga, the *jihvāmūlīya*, the *upadhmānīya*, elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification (*vikāra*), the original form (*prakṛti*), the altered form (*vikṛti*), breath, sound, both, the vocal chords (*raṅga*), trembling (*kampa*), place of articulation (*sthāna*), effort (*prayatna*), opening of the mouth (*vivṛtti*), and pause (*virāma*).

"Vicakṣaṇaḥ" means one who knows distinctions. Since this much alone is insufficient for the knowledge of phonemes (*varṇa*), he qualifies him as "one who knows the division of words and their sequences" (*padakramavibhāgajña*). Words (*pada*) are those established by grammar; therein lies the knowledge of modified and natural nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. "Sequence" (*krama*) is that which was composed by the teacher Bābhravya, consisting of both the *saṃhitā* and the *pada* forms. Its "division" (*vibhāga*) consists of the various types of word-divisions and sequence-divisions. One who knows these is "one who knows them" (*tajjñaḥ*). Even with that much, because it is still insufficient, he says: "one who knows the specific details of accents and prosodic measures" (*svaramātrāviśeṣajña*).

Accents are the acute (*udātta*) and so forth; measures are the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and so forth. Their specific distinctions consist of particular accents caused by the preceding or following elements of stems and suffixes, as well as particular measures consisting of heaviness (*gurutva*), lightness (*laghutva*), evenness, one measure (*ekamātra*), two measures (*dvimātra*), three measures (*trimātra*), half a measure (*ardhamātra*), and so on; he who knows these is "one who knows them" (*tajjñaḥ*). || 2 ||

Since it was stated in the first verse that [the matter] is "as declared in the previous treatises," he explains the meaning of the term *pūrvaśāstra* (previous treatise): "Its characteristics are to be known from the *Prātiśākhyas* and, in some cases, from grammar;
namely, doubling (*dvitva*) and abhinidhāna, as well as the prohibition of those two, respectively. (Verse 3)

The *pūrvarūpa* of a voiced aspirate (*soṣman*), the addition of a voiced aspirate before a preceding sound, the prohibition of the *yama*, the *yamaniṣedha*, the *vivṛtti*, and the *svarabhakti*. (4)
The nasalized and non-nasalized phonemes, both in their original (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta) forms, as well as the visarga, the jihvāmūlīya, and the upadhmānīya, are elided. || 5 ||
The anusvāra, kampita, raṅga, short (hrasva), and protracted (pluta)—
these should generally be understood in their proper sequence by those expert in the order of phonemes.

Regarding the definition of "tallakṣaṇa": for the sake of knowing the *hal* (consonants) and so forth, even grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and other sciences should occasionally be studied. Although there exist other definitions such as those found in the *Śikṣā*, certain matters must be known from the *Prātiśākhya* itself; for it is said: "One who does not know the correct recitation has no authority for [the performance of] silent recitation (*japa*) and the like;
therefore, the *Prātiśākhya* should be studied for the sake of achieving correct recitation."

Because of this statement [in the *Prātiśākhya*], although many characteristics exist therein, he states with three and a half verses that only these many are to be known in the present context: "And doubling," etc. Regarding "doubling" (*dvitva*): there, doubling is the utterance of a single phoneme twice. "Abhinidhāna" is a name for the suppression of sound, another name for which is "doubling. The negation of those two is their non-existence. The second and fourth letters of each class (*varga*) are aspirated (*soṣman*). Their "prior form" consists of the firstness of the second letter and the thirdness of the fourth letter.

*Soṣman*: the addition of a *soṣman* (aspirated sound) to a preceding [consonant]. *Vargādyasya vargadvitīyatvam*: the substitution of the second letter of a *varga* for the first letter of that same *varga*. *Āgama*: the insertion of an additional phoneme between two phonemes. *Yamāḥ*: the insertion of a nasalized consonant identical to the preceding stop before a following nasalized stop. *Yamaniṣedhaḥ*: the non-occurrence of the *yama* substitution in certain instances where it would otherwise apply. *Vivṛttiḥ*: the opening of the vocal organs (*vivṛti*) between vowels, characterized by a specific duration (*mātrā*). *Svarabhaktayaḥ*: vowel fragments.

When *repha* (ṛ) and *lakāra* (ḷ) are followed by a consonant, there is an insertion of the intermediate sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*. *Nāsikya*s: although produced in the throat and other [articulatory locations], they are pronounced together with the nose. *Anāsika*s: those different from them. *Lupta*s: phonemes that are observed at the time of the *pada-pāṭha* but are not observed in the *saṃhitā-pāṭha*. *Prākṛta*s: those which maintain the same form in both [the *pada* and *saṃhitā*]. *Vaikṛta*s: those phonemes which, though observed at the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, undergo a change into a different phoneme in the *saṃhitā*. *Visarga*: the fifth sibilant (*ūṣman*) occurring after a vowel. *Jihvāmūlīya*: [the sibilant] produced at the root of the tongue.

The *upadhmānīya* is that which follows the sounds *ka* and *kha* and is accompanied by a half-*visarga*. The *anusvāra* is that which follows the sounds *pa* and *pha* and is accompanied by a half-*visarga*. The eighth *ūṣman* (aspirate) is that which follows a vowel and consists of a nasalized vowel or consonant, being distinct from ordinary vowels and consonants. The *kampa* arises from a circumflex accent (*svarita*) such as the *jātya* and others. The *raṅga* is a specific quality of nasality (*sānunāsikatva*) among the vowels. The *pluta* includes the rules for short and long vowels as well as the primary *pluta* [protracted] vowel.
The *hrasva* (short) refers to the shortening of a long vowel at the time of word-separation (*padakāla*), whereas in continuous recitation (*saṃhitā*) it remains long. || 3–6 ||
Among those that have been proposed, he states the definition of doubling (dvitva):
A consonant (*hal*) preceded by a vowel (*svara*), a nasal (*anusvāra*), or [the letter *r*], and followed by a consonant, undergoes doubling;
as do the first letters of the classes (*varga*) after *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*; and the stops (*sparśa*) after *l*, except for *r* and *h*. (7)

Regarding *svara*: vowels (*svarāḥ*), beginning with *a* and ending with *au*. Regarding *anusvāra*: as previously mentioned. A consonant (*hal*) beginning with any one of those [vowels or *anusvāra*]—from *ka* to *ha*—undergoes doubling when followed by a consonant (*hali*). Examples: *devebbyaḥ*, *akkhyat*, *aggram*, *āppyāyasva*, *assmākam*, *tassya*, *saṃśśyat*. Why specify "preceded by a vowel or *anusvāra*" (*svarānusvārapūrva*)? [In the example] *tvāvataḥ*, there is no doubling of the letter *ta*. [In the example] *bṛhadbhā bibhrataḥ*, there is no doubling of the letter *bha*. Why specify "consonant" (*hal*)? [In the example] *agne apām*, there is no doubling of the letter *pa*. (Note: The rule applies to the doubling of a consonant that follows a vowel or *anusvāra* when another consonant follows it.)

What is the purpose of the phrase "hal-paraḥ" (followed by a consonant)? [Example: *to... śannāsaḥ*? [Answer: It is not so for *ta* and *tha*. Regarding the rule *śa-ṣa-se-ti*: ten consonants—the first members of the five classes (*ka-kha*, *ca-cha*, *ṭa-ṭha*, *ta-tha*, *pa-pha*)—undergo doubling when they follow *śa*, *ṣa*, or *sa* that are preceded by vowels or *anusvāra*. [Examples: *divaścit*; *yajuṣkṛtam*; *taskaram*. Why "preceded by vowels or *anusvāra*"? [Counter-example: *yatsthaḥ*. Why "not for *tha*"? [Because it follows] *śa* or *ṣa*. Why? [Example: *sapta*. Why "not for *ta*"? [Because it follows] a class-initial. Why? [Example: *pra śyāvāśva*. Why "not for *ya*"? [Because it follows] *la*; [consonants following] *la* become *sparśas* (stops).

The letters from *ka* to *ma* follow an *l* that is preceded by a vowel or an *anusvāra*. As in: *ulkām-iva*, *ulbbam*. Why "preceded by a vowel"? [Counter-example: *kulyāḥ*. Why "after an *l*"? [Counter-example: *apāṃ...* Why "of *na*"? [Counter-example: (preceded by a vowel etc. *mṛgyam*. Regarding *ra* and *ha*: consonants following *ra* and *ha* that are themselves preceded by a vowel or an *anusvāra* are doubled. As in: *arvvāk*, *vih‌yyakhyam*. Why "preceded by a vowel etc."? [Counter-example: *hvayāmi*. Why "of *va*"? [Counter-example: *rahayo...* Why "consonants"? [Counter-example: *ā tvā*. Why "consonants"? [Counter-example: *narāvāśaṃsam*. [In] *ahāvyagne*, there is no doubling of the letter *ā*. 7.
But *saṃyukta*, *ūṣman*, *tvam*, and *upadha* [do not undergo elision]; nor do *naṅ* and *au* when they stand at the end of a word before a vowel.
However, when not at the end of a word, *cha* is elided after a long vowel, and *cha* is also optionally elided after a short vowel following *m*.

(Regarding the term *saṃyukta*): A sibilant (*ūṣman*) that is conjoined [with another consonant] and does not have a vowel as its *upadhā* (penultimate letter), provided it is preceded by a non-existent [consonant] and followed by a consonant (*hal*), is doubled; this applies to the sibilants *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. Examples: *h hvayāmi*, *ś śyāvāśvasya*, *s stuṣe*. Why "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*)? [Counter-example: *sa naḥ*; here, the *s* is not doubled. Why "sibilant" (*ūṣman*)? [Counter-example: *tvāvataḥ*; here, the *t* is not doubled. Why "not having a vowel as its *upadhā*" (*anupadha*)? [Counter-example: *astu*; here, the *s* is not doubled. The suffixes *na* and *ṅ* following a short vowel are doubled when they stand at the end of a word and a vowel follows them; that is, *na* and *ṅ* occurring at the end of a word after a short vowel are doubled when a vowel follows. Examples: *han nacyutacyut*, *sadṛṅ ṅasi*. Why "at the end of a word" (*antaga*)? [Counter-example: *anarvāṇam*.

Why [specify] "after a short vowel"? [Example: *etāvān asya* (so great is he). Why [specify] "in a vowel"? [Example: *arhan bibharṣi* (O Worthy One, you bear). [Also: *sadhriyaṅ coda-vardhe*. But after a long vowel, *cha* occurs at the end of a word; however, when *cha* follows a long vowel in the middle of a word, it is doubled. [Examples: *aicchāma*, *aucchat*. Why "at the end of a word"? [Example: *varmaṇā chādayāmi* (I cover with armor). The particle *tu* is used for restriction; because doubling is prescribed everywhere at the end of a word, [the rule] "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāc chaḥ*) is formulated as a separate sūtra so that *cha* following a short vowel is doubled both at the end and in the middle of a word. [Example: *acchā vada*.

[The letter *cha*] is doubled as if after a shadow [i.e., immediately following], when it follows a short vowel. Why [say "short"]? As in: *varmaṇā chādayāmi* ("I cover with armor"). Or rather, [it is doubled] even when followed by *mā*; the rule is begun for the sake of [the case where *cha*] occurs at the end of a word following a long vowel. After the word *mā*, the letter *cha* is doubled: *mā cchedma* ("May we not cut off"). Why [say *mā*]? As in: *varmaṇā chādayāmi*. || 8 ||

Regarding this [sandhi], he states the prohibition of doubling that would otherwise apply by the rule *hrasvāc chaḥ*: "Except for *sahāti-hāyayasya*, there is no doubling; nor is there doubling for *tane* when it follows *pavamāna*.

Furthermore, a spirant (*ūṣman*) followed by a vowel or another spirant is doubled, as is a consonant (*krama*) that is the final member of a cluster (*upadha*) and is homogeneous with its own class (*svasavarṇa*). (9)

*saha* [is an exception]. *Saha*; *saha chandasaḥ*. *Atihāya chidrā*. *Yasya chāyā*. *Tane ca chardiḥ*. Why two? [As in] *madhvicca cchadyāt*. *Pavamāna chandasyam*. Why from these? [As in] *upa cchāyām iva*. And a spirant (*ūṣman*) followed by a vowel (*svara*) or a spirant is not doubled; the word "not" (*na*) carries over. A spirant—whether followed by a vowel or followed by another spirant (the spirants being *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*)—is not doubled. This is an exception to what would have been obtained by the rule for vowels and *anusvāra* ("*rahayor halaḥ*"). Examples where it is followed by a vowel: *yadadya*, *karhi*, *adarśi*, *parṣi*.

[The doubling of a consonant does not occur] when followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*): *yaśśukta iva*, *divassamrājā*, *devīpṣaṭ*. [It does not occur] when a vowel is followed by a sibilant: *kim? utve hradā iva*, *adarśyāyatī*, *varṣṣyām̐3 aha*, *prasarsrāṇasya*. Why "sibilant"? [Observe: *vattso mātṝḥ*. There is no prohibition for the letter *t*. [Regarding the rule] "its own homogeneous sound" (*svasavarṇaḥ*); the word "not" (*na*) carries over. When its own homogeneous sound is followed by its own homogeneous sound, it is not doubled: *annam*, *avaviddham*. Why "its own homogeneous sound"? [Observe: *amatthnādanyat*. [Regarding the rule] "having a semivowel as a preceding element" (*kramopadhaḥ*); the word "not" (*na*) carries over.
A phoneme that serves as the cause for doubling is not itself doubled. As in *arvvāk* and *as‌tteva*; because the *r* and *s* are the causes for doubling, they themselves do not undergo doubling. 9.
When followed by a consonant of its own class or by another [consonant], the final letter of a class does not [occur]; likewise, a final consonant at the end of a word [does not occur].

A stop, the letter *r*, or a semivowel (*yaṇ*) [is elided] before a stop; and stops other than the last [of their respective classes], as well as semivowels and sibilants (*uṣman*), [are elided] before a sibilant.

At the end of a word, a consonant (hal) is called abhinidhāna; likewise, a consonant following a semi-vowel (yaṇ) before another semi-vowel at the pause (virāma). This occurs except when it assumes a third state, or when there is no substitution, or before a homogeneous vowel (savarṇa). || 11 ||

(Regarding the term *vargya*: When followed by a letter belonging to its own class (*vargya*), a final letter of a class (*vargāntya*) is not doubled; provided that it is followed by a contact consonant (*sparśa*) belonging to its own class other than the fifth (*pañcama*). Thus, *ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m* are not doubled. Examples: *kaṅkataḥ*, *pṛñcatīḥ*, *āṇḍeva*, *bhavantu*, *taṃ brahmāṇam*. Why "followed by its own class member"? Consider *vammrakaḥ*. Why "final letter of a class"? Consider *ratnadhātamaṃ*. The repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*) is for the purpose of indicating a specific rule. A consonant at the end of a word (*padānta*) is likewise [not doubled]; a *hal* situated at the end of a word is not doubled. Example: *vark*.

Even when following a *repha* (r), why is it not doubled for *ka*? *vark*. Even when following a *repha*, why is it not doubled for *ka*? What is the purpose of the condition "at the end of a word" (*padānte*)? [Example: *okkye*. He states the definition of *abhinidhāna*: "A *sparśa* (stop) and a *yaṇ* (semivowel) other than *repha*, before a *sparśa*, [undergo] *abhinidhāna*. This means that *sparśas* located at the end of a word, and *yaṇs* excluding *repha*—namely *ya*, *la*, and *va*—become what is called *abhinidhāna* when followed by a *sparśa*. Examples: *vāk pataṅgāya*; *vaṣaṭ kṛtasya*; *teṣām pāhi*; *bhūridāvnaḥ*; *grāvṇām*; *ulbam*. Being at the end of a word is not possible for a *yaṇ*.

This is because of the statement: "The sibilants (ūṣman), the semivowels (antaḥstha), the *ṛ*-sounds, the sibilants (*uṣman*), and the *ca*-group do not reach the end [of the word]. Why say "except for *r*"? [Consider the example: *arcantaḥ*. There should be *abhinidhāna* of the *r*. It does not occur between two vowels. Some say that the term "at the end of a word" (*padānta*) does not carry over here; but that is not correct, because in cases where doubling occurs at the end of a non-word, such as in *agnim*, there would result the occurrence of *abhinidhāna*. Non-final consonants (*sparśa*) [are doubled] before a semivowel (*yaṇ*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*); at the end of a word, they are called *abhinidhāna*.

The *sparśa* (stop) consonants from *ka* to *bha*, when occurring at the end of a word and followed by the semivowels (*yaṇ*), sibilants (*ūṣman*), or *y*, *v*, *l*, *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*, are called *abhinidhāna*. Examples: *yad yad yāmi*; *vaṣaḍ vaṣaḍ*; *tān vaḥ*; *arvāk śaphāviva*; *tat savituḥ*. Why "stops" (*sparśāḥ*)? [Counter-example: *sindhuryat* (here *yat* is not a stop). Why "not after *ra*" (*rasya na*)? [Counter-example: *vatsaḥ* (here *sa* follows *ra*). Why "at the end of a word" (*padānte*)? [Counter-example: *tasya* (here *sa* is not at the end of a word). Why "non-final" (*anantyaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *samrājñī adhi* (here *jñ* is final). Why "not after *ma*" (*masya na*)? [Counter-example: *tatte* (here *te* follows *ma*). Why "semivowels and sibilants" (*yaṇūṣmaṇoḥ*)? [Counter-example: *tasya* (here *ya* is not a semivowel or sibilant).

If it is argued: "Why not discard the separate rules—*sparśārephayaṇaḥ sparśe padānte'bhinidhānākhyāḥ* and *anantyasparśā yaṇūṣmaṇoḥ padānte'bhinidhānākhyāḥ*—and instead create a single rule: *sparśayaṇāṃ sparśayaṇūṣmasu*? The answer is: No; for then in the cases of *arvāgdevāḥ* and *samrājñī*, the rule would incorrectly entail *abhinidhāna* (doubling) of the *repha* and the vowel *a*. Regarding the rule *hal virāme*: a consonant (*hal*) followed by a pause (*avasāna*) is called *abhinidhāna*. Examples: *āgamat*; *manāṃsi jānatām*.

What [is the result] at the end? *yadadya* | *dasya na* | *yaṇo yaṇi*; [the consonants] *ya*, *la*, and *va* located at the end of a word—whether nasalized (*sānunāsika*) or not, whether modified (*vaikṛta*) or original (*prākṛta*)—are called *abhinidhāna* when followed by a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) *ya*, *la*, or *va*. Examples: *yayyum̐jam*, *tavvam̐ indram*, *eṣāllam̐kṣmīḥ*. [The rule] does not apply to a *repha* (r) when followed by a *repha*; in that case, there is elision of the preceding [sound]. Why "at the end of a word"? [Example: *te rayyā*. *yasya na*.

In the rule "sparśārephayaṇaḥ sparśe" (a *sparśa* or *yaṇ* [is doubled] before a *sparśa*), because the author does not say "sparśayaṇoḥ" but instead treats "yaṇo yaṇi" as a separate rule, the prohibition to be stated later—"nādeśasvasavarṇayoḥ" (there is no doubling of a substitute or of a homogeneous vowel)—does not apply here. He states the prohibition regarding *abhinidhāna* (the suppression of breath): "Because of the state of being the third. When followed by a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) consonant, the state of being the third [of their respective classes] belongs to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*—namely, *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, and *ba*. Without that [state], there is no *abhinidhāna* of the substituted letter. Examples: *tvaṃ karañjam* (you, the *karañja* tree); *sañjahan te* (striking you). Why "of a substitute"? [Consider: *teṣāmpādi*. (Here, the doubling occurs because it is not a substitute.)

Even in the absence of an explicit rule, *abhinidhāna* (nasalization) occurs because of the absence of an alternative instruction. [This applies] when there is a homogeneous sound (*svasavarṇa*), meaning a sound of the same class within its own varga. In the case of *tat te*, because the rule for the *sparśa* (stop) series does not apply across different positions, *abhinidhāna* does not occur. Why "when there is a homogeneous sound"? Consider the example: *teṣāṃ pāhi*. 10, 11.
When a sibilant (ūṣman) is subject to doubling, that which precedes it is pronounced once;
at the end of a word, the second [consonant] shall be the first of its class when followed by a sibilant. (12)

Regarding the term *soṣman* (aspirated): when a doubling (*dvitva*) is to occur for an aspirated sound, that which precedes it is pronounced once. When doubling applies to the second and fourth letters of the classes—namely *kh, gh, ch, jh, ṭh, ḍh, th, dh, ph, bh*—in the first utterance, the first letters of the second class (*k, c, ṭ, t, p*) and the third letters of the fourth class (*g, j, ḍ, d, b*) shall take their place. Examples: *ak-khyat*, *ac-cha*, *avāḍ-ḍhavyāni*, *rat-thyeva*, *ab-bhrāteva*. Why "of an aspirated sound"? [Consider: *agn-e*. Why "not at the end of a word"? [Consider: *vāk* (where *k* remains).

A letter standing in the middle of a word that is the first of its class shall become the second [letter of that class] when followed by a sibilant (ūṣman). Examples: *vatthyō*, *mātṝḥ*, *vṛkkhṣe*, *virapphśī*. Why "not at the end of a word"? As in *tatsavituh*. || 12 ||
He states the augmentations (āgamas): "An *oṣṭhya* [consonant] followed by a non-*oṣṭhya* vowel receives the *kaṇṭhya* augment *va*.
In the case of *na* and *ṭa*, there is the augment *ta* before *sa*; in the case of *ṅa* and *ña*, there is *śa* before *śara*; and in the case of *ka* and *ca*, there is *kaca*. (13)

Regarding the rule *oṣṭhyajātasya*: when vowels produced from the labial sounds *o* and *au*—namely *a* and *ā*—are followed by the dissimilar vowels *u*, *ū*, *o*, or *au*, the augment *va* is inserted between them. Examples: *vāyav indraḥ*; *tāv indrāgnī*. Why "produced from a labial" (*oṣṭhyajātasya*)? Example: *asmā uṣāsaḥ*. Why "of the guttural" (*kaṇṭhyasya*)? Example: *pito ajagan*. Why "not [followed] by a non-labial" (*anoṣṭhye*)? Example: *vāya ukthebhiḥ*; *ubhā u nūnam*. Regarding the rule *naṭayoḥ se takāraḥ syāt*: when the letter *s* follows, the augment *t* is inserted between the letters *n* and *ṭ*. Examples: *sasavāntsantsūyase*; *virāṭtsamrāṭ*.

What is the purpose of the rule regarding *ṇa* and *ta*? [To show: *tat sūryam*. Why is it said "after *se*"? [To show: *tān vaḥ*. When *śar* follows *ṅa* or *ña*, *śa* is replaced by *ka* and *ca* respectively; that is, among *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*, *ṅa* becomes *ka*, and *ña* becomes *ca*. [Examples: *arvāṅ k chaśvattamam*; *pratyaṅ k saḥ*; *vajriṅ c chaśnathihi*; *maghavaṅ c chagghi*. In these cases, the substitution (*ch*) occurs immediately after the augment (*āgama*). Why is it said "when *śar* follows"? [To show: *dadhyaṅ ha*; *pratyaṅ citrā*. Why is it said "when *śa* follows"? [To show: *śañ cayos ca*. (13)
In the middle of those two *hṛdayas*, and in the middle of the *pada*s, the letters *ka* and *ga* occur in sequence;
likewise, in the verse (*padya*) of the words *puruṣṛthva* and *adhi*, as well as in the preceding *pada*. (14)
When followed by *candra*, the letter *ś* becomes *ṣ*; likewise, *sakāra* [becomes *ṣ*] before *askṛta-uṣasam*.

In the word *pari*, it becomes *ṣ* before a *kṛ* beginning with a *p* (i.e., *parikṛ*), but not when the *kṛ* begins with a non-*p* (i.e., *aparikṛ*); and when followed by another *kṛ*, it becomes *ṣ*. (15)

Regarding "between those two marked with ṅ": in the domain of non-word-final [consonants], *k* is inserted between *ṅ* and *t*, and *g* is inserted between *ṅ* and *dh*. Examples: *yuṅkte*, *yuṅgdhvam*. Why "in the middle of a word"? [Counter-example: *puru-pṛthu-adhi*; in this three-word sequence, when any preceding word is followed by *candra*, the augment *ś* is inserted in the middle. Examples: *puruścandraṃ yajatam*, *pṛthuścandram avase*, *adhiścandraṃ bṛhat*, *hariścandraḥ*, *suścandraḥ*. Why "of *puru* and the others"? [Counter-example: *abhicandrā*.

What follows *candra*? *adhisānau*, *puruvīram*. What follows *padye*? *abhi candrā*. What follows *candre*? *kavikratuḥ*. Regarding the letter *s*: when the word *akṛta* follows the word *uṣasam* at the time of the *padapāṭha*, there is the addition of the letter *s* in *saṃhitā* when the word *uṣasam* follows. What follows *uṣasam*? *cintyam*. Regarding *parītīti*: in a two-part word (*dvikhaṇḍapada*), after the word *pari*, there is the addition of the letter *ṣ* below the syllable *kṛ*. Example: *pariṣkṛṇvan*. What follows *kṛpare*? *paridāya*. What follows *padye*? What follows *pari*? *cintyam*.

The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the word *kṛṇvanti* when it follows the word *pari*, provided that the two words remain separate. For example: *pariṣkṛṇvanti*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *kṛṇvanti*? As in: *pari suvānaḥ*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *pari*? This must be investigated (*mṛgyam*). 14,15.

Likewise, in the case of *vanarṣade*, these same four—the consonants beginning with *ka*—are indeed the augmenting *repha*s when followed by the final letters of their respective classes (*vargāntya*). || 16 ||
The *sparśa* consonants attain the same nature as the following vowel, whether it be voiced (*sayama*) or nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
When joined with the first [vowels], they remain the first; likewise, when joined with the second and subsequent vowels, they follow that order respectively. (17)

"So be it. Thus, there is a *repha* (the letter *r*) in "vanarṣade"; that is to say, it consists of two parts. Regarding "vanarṣadam": these alone are indeed the augmentations (*āgama*s). From the rule beginning with "of that which is born from a labial" up to "so be it... in *vanarṣade*," these are precisely the augmentations stated in the *Prātiśākhya*. Because of this restriction, in cases such as "babhūva," the augmentations like *vuk* mentioned in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) are not to be accepted, since they are not mentioned in the *Prātiśākhya*. He states the definition of the *yamala* (twins): "four," etc.

The first four consonants of each class—*ka, kha, ga, gha; ca, cha, ja, jha; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha; ta, tha, da, dha; pa, pha, ba, bha*—constitute the twenty *sparśas* (stops). When followed by any final consonant of their respective class (*ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m*), these stops undergo a change into another sound called *yama*, which is similar to itself but nasalized. Examples: *palikkam̐nīḥ*, *cakhkham̐khnatuḥ*, *aggam̐man*, *vṛtraghgham̐ne*, *parijjam̐mānamiva*, *rattam̐nadhātamam*, *āttam̐mānam*, *āppnām̐nam*. Why "stops"? [As in] *brahmā*, *dadhikrāvṇaḥ*.

What are the four? *arvāṅ narāḥ*. Why [is it said] "in the case of the finals of the classes"? [Consider] *arvāg devāḥ*. Since there are twenty non-fifth consonants (*apañcamasparśa*), and since their conjunction with the five class-finals results in one hundred varieties, it would follow that the *yamas* (nasalized counterparts) should also have a hundred-fold designation; therefore, he states that their designation is indeed fourfold: "the first," etc. This means that when the first members of the classes—*ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa*—are joined with a fifth [consonant], they are the first *yama*; when the second members are joined with the fifths, they are the second *yama*, and so forth. On this point, some maintain that what is called a *yama* is not a distinct phoneme.

"But [some argue] that *yama* is merely a specific quality of the preceding phoneme itself, consisting of an additional half-mora duration and nasality; that is not so, because it is enumerated as a distinct entity among the sixty-four phonemes in the *Pāṇinīyaśikṣā* and other such works, and is therefore indeed a different phoneme. (16, 17)
He states the prohibition regarding *yama*:
"There is never an occurrence of *yama* for a *sparśa* (stop consonant) produced by heat (*ūṣman*).
That [occurrence] is a fourfold expansion (*vivṛtti*) occurring between vowels that lack a *saṃdhi*. (18)

"No. There is no *yama* for a *sparśa* produced in the place of a sibilant (*ūṣman*). [As in the example] *pradodhuvat śmaśruṣu*. Here, between the two *cha*s, there is no second *yama*, because the *cha* has the *śa* as its place of articulation (*sthāna*). He explains *vivṛtti*: "fourfold. *Vivṛtti* is that which stands between two vowels, devoid of the junction (*saṃdhi*) of preceding and following sounds. || 18 ||
He says that it is fourfold:
short-long, short-short-long, long-short-long, and both long and short in sequence.
Some say that *pākavatī* has two short [syllables] and both [others] have two long [syllables], while *pipīlikā* has [all] long [syllables]. 19.

"Long at the beginning, such as *vatsānusāryā* etc.; long at the end, such as *vatsānusṛti*; short in both places"—the word "both" (*ubhaya*) applies everywhere. Short in both places is *vivṛtti*. Short on both sides is likewise [called] "long in both. But that which is short-long in both is "long at the end"; that which is long-short in both is "long at the beginning," as in *pratyu adarśi*, *kā ūrū*, *agna ā*, and *agne apām*. He states another alternative: "some say"—that which has the *pāka* [accent] is short in both places; that which has both [accents] long is *pipīlikā*. Regarding *vatsa*: "long at the beginning, such as *vatsānusāryā* etc.; long at the end, such as *vatsānusṛti*."
The meaning is that they say: "That which has a long initial vowel is 'vatsānusāriṇī' (following the calf), and that which has a long final vowel is 'vatsānusṛtiḥ' (the calf's following). || 19 ||
When a *repha* (the sound *r*) is preceded by a vowel and followed by a consonant, it stands in the middle of those two.

The svarabhakti (vowel-fragment) following an *ṛ* or *ṝ* should be long; likewise, it should be so when following an *l* or a sibilant (*ūṣman*). It is to be known as longer in the case of a long vowel sequence, and shorter otherwise.

He explains *svarabhakti* (the vowel-fragment) with the words "beginning with a vowel" (*svareti*). When a *repha* (the sound *r*) preceded by a vowel occurs before a consonant (*hal*), there is an augment in the form of *ṛ* called *svarabhakti*. When an *l* preceded by a vowel occurs before a sibilant (*ūṣman*), there is a *svarabhakti* in the form of *ḷ*. Examples are: *arṛcchanti*, *jallṛhavaḥ*, and *sahasravallṛśāḥ*. Because the *svarabhakti* is a distinct phoneme, he states its specific duration: "longer" (*drāghīyasī*). When the following consonant is not doubled, the *svarabhakti* has a duration of half a *mātrā* and is designated as "longer. Examples are: *karṛhi* and *parṛrṣi*.

Regarding the doubling [of consonants] obtained by the rule *rahayorhalaḥ*, there is a prohibition by the rule *svaroṣmapara ūṣmā tu*; thus, there is no doubling for *ha* and *ṣa*. Consequently, the *svarabhakti* preceding those two is longer (*drāghīyasī*). However, in cases where a following consonant is doubled, it is shorter (*hrasīyasī*) and is designated as having the measure of one quarter (*pādamātrā*). In *adarśśyā yatī*, because of the doubling of *śa* by the rule *rahayorhalaḥ*, the *svarabhakti* preceding it is shorter. (20, 21)
With the arising of its heat (ūṣman), there is a fivefold designation due to the differentiation of color:
through the letters *ra* and *la*, and in the case of the letter *ha*, they are respectively *kareṇu* and *karviṇī*. (22)
When *śa* or *sa* follows, it is *hariṇī*; when *śa* follows *ra* or *la*, it is *dhāriṇī*. When *ha* follows *ra* and *ṣa* follows, it becomes *haṃsapadā*. (23)

Regarding "of that" (*tasyāḥ*), there are five types of designations when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) arises from a vowel-syllable (*svarabhakti*). He states those very [designations] as "with *repha*" (*repha-iti*). When *ra* and *la*, preceded by a vowel, are followed by *ha*, they respectively become *karemuḥ* and *karviṇī*: *ar-ṛhan*. When *ra* is followed by *śa* or *sa*, it becomes *hariṇī*: *adar-ṛśyāyatī*; *prasar-ṛtrāṇasya*. When *la* is followed by *śa*, it becomes *hāriṇī*: *śatavall-ṛśaḥ*. When *ra* is followed by *ṣa*, it becomes *haṃsapadā*: *sahastraśīr-ṛṣā*.

Some phonemes are exclusively nasalized, some are exclusively non-nasalized, and some are of both kinds due to a difference in duration. The first are those articulated in their own place of articulation together with the nose; the second are those arising from their own place of articulation alone; the third are of both kinds. (22, 23)
Regarding that, he states the third [set]: "In the place of *ya* and *va*, there are substitutes (*ādeśa*) at the end of a word which are nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
They are non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) when they are distinct from the *yama*s, the *anusvāra*, and the final letters of the [five] classes (*varga*). (24)

Regarding *yavala*: at the end of a word (*padānte*), the sounds *ya*, *va*, and *la* which take the place of nasalized vowels (*sānunāsika-varṇa*) shall become nasalized (*sānunāsika*) when followed by *ya*, *va*, or *la* respectively. Examples: *yayyaṃ*, *tavvaṃḥ*, *eṣāllaṃkṣmīḥ*. Here, the preceding *ya*, *va*, and *la* are nasalized because they take the place of nasalized vowels; the subsequent ones are non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). Thus, the *ya*, *va*, and *la* sounds are of two kinds. What is meant by "taking the place of a nasalized vowel"? Example: *aṅgādaṅgāllomno lomnaḥ*. Why "respectively" (*yathākramam*)? Example: *kravyādam*.

Having stated both types of vowels, he speaks of those that are exclusively nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and those that are exclusively non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). He says "the *yamās*": there are four *yamās*, the *anusvāra*, and *ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m*; these ten are exclusively nasalized. The *ya, va, la* [semivowels] and the vowels are of both kinds. All other phonemes (*varṇas*) are exclusively non-nasalized. He will explain another nasalized sound among the vowels in the context of *raṅga*. (24)
He states [the examples] of elided vowels:
"By the expansion of consciousness, he is elided; *pīvaḥ*, *annām̐ḥ*, *rayivṛdhaḥ*;
*dadhanvām̐yaḥ*, *jujurvām̐yaḥ*, *svavām̐ya*, *ātu*, *dadvām̐va*" (RV 10.89.4). || 25 ||

Regarding the word *cit*: the letter *s* seen at the time of the *pada-pāṭha* in *cit skambhanena* is termed "elided" (*lupta*) because it is not seen in the *saṃhitā-pāṭha* as *citkambhanena*. Similarly, the letter *n* [is elided] in such cases as *pīvo annām̐ rayivṛdhaḥ*. 25.
Between the vowel and the consonant, the elided *n* is joined again:
"rathaṃ riṇanti" and "vivyāca gāvo garbhaṃ mṛjanti. (26)
Friends, let us go beyond the calf; let him not be one whose consciousness is lost.
And the irregular forms [occur] due to the substitution of the nasalized vowel (ādeśa) following the conduct of the third cowherd. || 27 ||

Regarding *ākāra*: when the letter *na* preceded by *ā* occurs at the end of a word, it is not seen in *saṃhitā* before a vowel; that too is called "elided. Examples: *tāṃ indra*, *marutvāṃ indra*. Why say "preceded by *ā*"? [Observe: *arhann agne*. Why say "before a vowel"? [Observe: *tān vaḥ*. Why say "at the end of a word"? [Observe: *nānānam*. Regarding *pṛcyate*: when *pṛcyate* and the following words occur, the elided form *īm-makāra* [is applied]. Examples: *samī pṛcyate*, *jagdhamī punaḥ*, *samī ratham*, *e riṇanti*, *samī vivyā ca*, *samī gāvaḥ*.

*yamī garbham* | *tamī mṛjanti* | *samī vatsam* | *samī sakhāyaḥ*. What about these? *samīṃ rebhāsaḥ*, *sa īṃ rebho na*. Regarding the modified consonants (*vaikṛtavarṇa*), he says: "The third. When followed by a vowel or a voiced consonant (*ghoṣa*), the *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa* series respectively become *ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba*; these are the "third" sounds. *te tṛtīyagāḥ*. *tadindrasya*, *yadvāgvadanti*. At the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, when *visarga* is followed by *ka, kha, pa, pha*, those *sa* and *ṣa* sounds [resulting from the sandhi] are treated as *upācarita* (modified) in *saṃhitā*: *divaspari*, *svāduṣkila*.

At the time of the *pada* recitation, the following substitutions (*ādeśa*) are applied to the [words] beginning with *ṣaṇ*, *ḍa*, and *ḍha*: *suṣuma*, *mo ṣu naḥ*, *dūḍabhaḥ*, and *dūḍhye*. Apart from those [cases] where the third letter [of a word] is modified according to the rules for *gopā* and *carita*, whatever phonemes undergo a change into a different phoneme at the time of the *saṃhitā* recitation—wherever they become another phoneme—that other phoneme is called a substitution (*ādeśa*). Examples include *yaṅ krandasī*, *tañ citrayāmam*, *tantte*, and *tayam̐yajñam*. These phonemes beginning with the third letter are "modified" (*vaikṛta*).

Although these [substitutions] beginning with the third letter are also technically *ādeśas*, they are mentioned separately for the sake of variety and to facilitate the knowledge of their specific forms. (Sūtras 26, 27)
Others than those should be known as *prākṛta*, even those arising from the root of words (*padaprakṛti*).
The *visarga* is of three kinds: *lupta*, *prākṛta*, and *vaikṛta*. (28)
A consonant situated between *h*, *y*, *e*, *ś*, *s*, and *y*, as well as a sibilant (*ūṣman*) followed by an unvoiced sound (*aghoṣa*), and a *visarga* are designated as elided (*lupta*). (29)

Regarding the phrase "other than that": the phonemes (*varṇa*) that are identical in form between two words joined in *saṃhitā* are called *prākṛta* (original). For example, in *agnim īḷe* and *yān vaḥ naraḥ*, the phonemes are *prākṛta*. In the context of a word (*pada*), those phonemes which undergo a change into other phonemes within the domain of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) are called *padaprakṛtijāḥ* (born from the original form of the word). These too are indeed *prākṛta*. In examples such as *babhūva* and *pibati*, there is a modification of the base; in *bhavāmi* and *bhavanti*, there is a modification of the suffix; and in *jahī*, there is a modification of both. One should not suspect that these [latter] are *vaikṛta* (modified) either.

Because of the non-derivation [of phonetic changes] by grammar (*vyākaraṇāsiddhatva*), the time of the word (*pada*) and the time of the *saṃhitā* are of one form; for, in comparison with the time of the word, it is precisely at the time of the *saṃhitā* that the phonemes (*varṇa*), which possess different forms, are considered modified (*vaikṛta*). Although the distinction between the modified (*vaikṛta*) and the original (*prākṛta*) also exists regarding accents (*svara*), it is not set forth here because such usage is not observed and for fear of making the book too voluminous. "Visarga" is threefold due to the division of the elided original (*luptaprākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*). The word "tu" has the sense of "only" (*eva*). The word "iti" is intended to indicate the twofold nature of the modified (*vaikṛta*).

Regarding that, he states what is elided: *hali*. This means that when *visarga* follows [the words] *eṣaḥ*, *saḥ*, or *syaḥ*, it is elided before a consonant (*hal*), and is thus termed "elided. Examples: *eṣa devaḥ*; *sa devaḥ*; *uta sya vājī*. Why "before a consonant"? [Example: *eṣa indrāya*; *sa it*. Here, although the *visarga* is not visible, by the rule "but when preceded by a short vowel, *sa-* becomes *akāra*," the *visarga* with the preceding *s-* is replaced by the letter *a*. Regarding "situated in the middle": at the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, that *visarga* which was preceded by a vowel and followed by *repha* (r) but is no longer seen, is also considered "elided. Example: *pṛthū rathaḥ*.

What is the purpose of the condition "followed by *r*"? [Example: *viṣṇuryat*. Regarding the rule "when followed by a voiceless sound" (*aghoṣe*): the *visarga* is elided even when followed by a sibilant (*ūṣman*) that is itself followed by a voiceless sound. [Example: *samudra sthaḥ*. What is the purpose of the condition "followed by a voiceless sound"? [Example: *devāsaḥ sarvayā*. What is the purpose of the condition "final sibilant" (*ūṣmāntya*)? [Example: *devāstam*. (28, 29)
He states the Prākṛta rule: In the Pada-pāṭha and at a pause, the *k* [of *catuḥ*] becomes *c* before *kh* followed by *r*,
as in *caturaścakre*, *carati*, *cikitvān*, and *camasāṃśca co*.
O most excellent one, you move with vigor among men; you are the self-strong protector, the vessel.
All those [beings], all those gods—do you protect them, and do you yourself speak out for them. 31.

For the lords of men (*nṛm̐ḥpatibhyaḥ*), for the leader of men (*nṛm̐ḥpraṇetram*), and for the protection of men (*nṛm̐ḥpāhi*); in these examples, when a non-aspirated consonant belonging to the first or last class follows, the *visarga* undergoes a modification (*vaikṛta*) according to the sequence.

The letters *ka* and *pa* become *uṣman* sounds when they follow a consonant that has no following vowel; likewise, the *anusvāra* of *ma* becomes *repha* (*ṛ*) before the directions *iṅgī*, *samrāj*, and *vinādi*.

He states: "In the *padapāṭha*, the *visarga* that occurs is the natural (*prākṛta*) one. For example: *agniḥ pūrvebhiḥ*, *puraḥ hitam*, *citraśravastamaḥ*. Although this is established by the rule for the pause (*virāma*), it is mentioned separately as "the *padapāṭha*" because in cases such as *purohitam*, a vowel-sandhi (*svarasaṃdhi*) is observed. And regarding the pause: a pause (*virāma*) is the absence of a subsequent phoneme. Compared to a duration less than one *mātrā*, when there is a phoneme after a duration of one *mātrā*—whether that phoneme exists or not—that *visarga* is the natural one.

"May you also blow a blessing upon our mind. (In this rule: when *kh* follows a *śar* [consonant], and when *k*, *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *p*; *kh*, *ch*, *ṭh*, *th*, *ph* follow, the *visarga* remains in its original (*prākṛta*) form. Examples: *ghanāghanaḥ kṣobhaṇaḥ*; *śatakratuḥ tthsarat*. Why "when *kh* follows a *śar*" (*śarpare*)? [Observe: *devāstam*. Why "when *kh*" (*khayi*)? [Observe: *devo devebhiḥ*. Regarding the modified (*vaikṛta*) *visarga*, he says: "in the case of *caturaḥ*," etc. When the ten words beginning with *caturaḥ* follow in *saṃhitā*, as well as the *visarga* found in cases such as *nṝm̐ḥ pātram*, the *visarga* is modified (*vaikṛta*).

In this *saṃhitā*, although the visarga may take the form of *śa* or *upadhmānīya*, it does not appear in the recitation of individual words (*padapāṭha*). Therefore, it must arise in place of the letter *n*. The phoneme produced therein is born from a modified visarga (*vaikṛtavisarga*), as in the following examples: *rāyaḥ samudrāṃś caturaḥ*; *tāṃś cakre*; *mahāṃś carati*; *vidvāṃś cikittvān*; *vibhrājamānāṃś camasān*; *asmāṃś ca tāṃś ca*; *yāṃś co nu*; *nṝṃś cyautnaḥ*; *mahāṃś carasi*; *tāṃś cid eva*; *kaditthā nṝṃḥ pātram*.

The protector is self-strong. May we obtain all those from you, O Indra. You are the encompasser of all those gods; protect them, O Victorious One. You spoke for the sake of the men’s wives regarding the womb; [you spoke] for the men’s praise, for the men’s leader. Protect the men; hear [us]. By the word "etc. (ādi), there is the reference to the meat-cooking pot (*ukhā*), or to the place where meat is cooked (*māṃścatva*), or to the redness of the meat-cooker (*bradhna māṃścatoḥ*). Since these three—beginning with the meat-cooking pot—are mentioned later in the context of the *raṅga* ritual, they are indicated here by the word "etc. (*ādi*).

In this context, among the ten [words] beginning with *catur*, there is the substitution of *ś* for the *visarga* produced by the letter *n*. In the thirteen words beginning with *nṝḥ pātram*, there is only the modified (*vaikṛta*) *visarga* produced by the letter *n*. This meaning is indicated by the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "but the modified... (*vaikṛtastu*). Regarding the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya, he says: "At the beginning and end... (*ādyanta-*). When followed by unvoiced consonants (*aghoṣa*) born from the first class (*ādivargaja*), namely *ka* or *kha*, the *visarga*—other than that which is the subject of the substitution of *s* or *ṣ*—becomes, respectively, *ka* and *kha*, accompanied by a half-*visarga*.

When followed by *pa* or *pha*, the gutturals (*ghoṣa*) born from the final class [the nasals] become *pa* and *pha* respectively, accompanied by a half-visarga (*ardhavisarga*). Examples: *ya kṛtantam*; *agastya khanamānaḥ*; *ya pañca*; *yā phalinīḥ*. Why "not preceded"? As in: *tavasaskṛtāni*; *divaspari*. Regarding the anusvāra: he says "anusvāra. When *ma* at the end of a word is followed by *ra* at the beginning of a word, there shall be the eighth sibilant (*ūṣman*), consisting of both vowel and consonant, provided it is not of the form *saṃpūrva-rāṭ* (which consists of two parts).

The meaning is: "except for that single word-form which takes all case-endings. Examples: *tvaṃ rājā* ("you are the king"). What is the purpose of [specifying] "the first" (*ādige*)? [Example: *varmakaḥ*. What is the purpose of "except for *iṅgya* and *samrāṭ*"? [Examples: *samrājñī adhi*. What is the purpose of "*iṅgya*" (meaning "a word ending in a vowel")? [Example: *saṃrājabhiḥ*. What is the purpose of "when *re* follows"? [Example: *tvañ cakartha*. (30–33)
In all cases where there is an arising of *uṣman*, it should likewise occur in the middle of a word;
at the end of a word it is called *paripan* (or *paripanna*), while in the middle of a word it is termed *vaikṛta*.

Regarding the term *sarvatra* (everywhere): at the end of a word (*padānte*) and in the middle of a word (*padamadhye*), when followed by the sibilants *ha*, *śa*, or *ṣa*, the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*. Examples: *saṃsam*, *tāṃ su*, *puṃsaḥ putrān*. Why [is it said] "when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) arises"? [Consider: *śañca*. Regarding the rule *nasya*: in the middle of a word, the nasal (*naḥ*) becomes an *anusvāra* when a sibilant arises. Examples: *vidvāṃsau*, *śreyāṃsam*, *vāvṛdhvāṃsam*, *haṃsaḥ*. Why [is it said] "in the middle of a word"? [Consider: *devān huve*. He states the distinction in technical names for the two types of *anusvāra*—that which replaces *m* and that which replaces *n*—by saying "at the end of a word": at the end of a word, the *anusvāra* resulting from *m* is established.

In the middle of a word, the anusvāra may be either nasalized (m) or non-nasalized (n); this is the modified form. The first type is, for example: *tvaṃ rājā* or *saṃ sam*. The second type is, for example: *puṃsaḥ*, *haṃsaḥ*, or *ye sahāṃsi*. 34.
He states the positions of the *kampa*:
"Those that are produced by birth (*jāti*), by being struck (*abhinihita*), by being hurried (*kṣepa*), and those that are closely joined (*paśliṣṭa*) participate in the *kampa*.
They are of two kinds: short and long, occurring at the rise of a *svarita*. (35)

Regarding the term *jātya*: among the seven types of *svarita* (circumflex) accents, such as *jāti*, *abhinihita*, *kṣepa*, *praśliṣṭa*, and so forth, four—namely those called *jāti*, *abhinihita*, *kṣepa*, and *praśliṣṭa*—are subject to modulation (*kampabhāj*). "A *yakāra* or a *vakāra* joined with consonants, whether preceded by nothing or preceded by a low-pitched (*nīca*) vowel, is called the *jāti-svara*."

Thus [it is asked]: "Where indeed? [The answer is: "Like a sickle. "When *e* and *o* are high-pitched (*udātta*) and the following *a* is low-pitched (*anudātta*), and if there is a *ya*-insertion (*payas*), where there occurs a unification (*ekībhāva*), that is called the *svāra-abhinihita* [sandhi]."
Thus they said: "A Brahmin [is the authority] on this:

'When the vowels *i* and *u* become udātta while *y* and *v* [remain] in certain cases, one should always recite them as anudātta; one should know this to be the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* [svarita]. "
Thus: *śruṣṭyagne*, *apsvagne*.
"If the vowel *i* is preceded by a high-pitched [vowel] and is followed by another *i* that is elided, the teachers who are experts in phonetics call this the *praśliṣṭa* (contracted) *svāra*."
"Then the teachers, who were experts in vowels and consonants, recited [the text] with phonetic coalescence (*praśliṣṭa*). This is the reading found in the printed *Ākara-kośa*.

Thus: *srucau iva ghṛtam*. In these four cases where a *svarita* is followed by another *svarita* or an *udātta*, there shall be a tremor (*kampa*). This tremor is of two kinds: when the preceding *svarita* is short, the tremor takes a short form; when it is long, it takes a long form. The short tremor (*hrasvakampa*) consists of one and a half *mātrās*; the long tremor (*dīrghakampa*) consists of three *mātrās*. By the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), the *raṅga* (intonation) to be described hereafter is also twofold, distinguished as short and long. An example of the natural tremor (*jātyakampa*) is: *kva3vo 'śvāḥ* ("Where are the horses?"), *kvā3bhīśavaḥ* ("Where are the reins?"), *tanvi3rephā ādhuḥ* ("The slender ones have placed the reed"), and *ahyo3 na cāravaḥ* ("Like serpents, they are not beautiful").

The *abhinihita-kampa* occurs, for example, in: *yathā-rathānāṃ3naye 3rāḥ | divi me anyaḥ pakṣo3dhaḥ*. When there is an *abhinihita*, the short-vowel *kampa* does not occur. The *kṣaipra-kampa* occurs, for example, in: *makṣvi3tthā | udīrṣvātaḥ pativatī hye3ṣā*. The *praśliṣṭa-kampa* occurs, for example, in: *tvāṃ hī3ndrāvase*. Even when there is a *praśliṣṭa*, the short-vowel *kampa* does not occur. All of these examples have been cited with an *udātta* vowel following. With a *svarita* vowel following, it is as in: *śatacakraṃ yo3hyo vartaniḥ*. What is the purpose of mentioning the *svarita* in the rule? [Answer: As in: *kva svidāsām*.
"Not in the same kind," they said. "A Brahmin is his [offspring]; he is the one who offers the oblation, the butter-drinker. O Agni, through obedience, [your fame] is like an eye in the sky. (35)
He states the *raṅga* [metre]: In the *pādādyaj* [section], the *raṅga* always consists of [the syllables] after the *kaṇṭhya* (gutturals) and *e-o*, following the elision (*luśāt*).
In these [cases], the final [syllable] belongs to *mitra* and *yuṣmad*; [the word] *namasyuḥ* and *carṣaṇīḥ* are [also] *īvat*. (36)
"To the people, for their pleasure, the highest station, the unsurpassed;
and to Gautama, they do not diminish"—thus [is it] in this circle of fires of Atri. 37.

Regarding *pāde*: when a vowel at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*) follows, the final vowel of the preceding word is designated as *raṅga*. For example: *mandiṣṭa yaduśane kāvye sacām indraḥ*. Why "at the beginning of a quarter-verse"? [Consider: *sa caiṣu*. Regarding *kaṇṭhyau*: from the verse beginning with *agnim īḷe* up until, but not including, the verse *abudhram u tya* by the seer Luśa, the vowels *a* and *ā* are *raṅgas* when followed by *e* or *o* at the beginning of a quarter-verse. Examples: *ā yan mā venā aruhan ṛtasya* (one *e*), *tisro dyāvaḥ savitur dvā upastham ekā* (one *o*).

"Thou, O Indra, hast brought us strength; every day [is] fierce, like power, [our] dwelling. From what [word] does this arise? From "luśāt": "He who by his greatness alone [rules over] all that breathes and blinks. Why "at the beginning of a pāda"? [As in: "mainam agne" (O Agni, do not [harm him]) and "amitaujāḥ" (of immeasurable power). The rule "in these cases" (*eṣu*) follows from the previous rule "after a vowel at the beginning of a pāda" (*pādādyaci*). After these words—ending in *e*, ending in *pu*, *mitrayoḥ*, *asmāt*, *namastuḥ*, *carṣaṇīḥ*, *īvat*, *carṣaṇibhyaḥ*, and *joṣam*—the word *ā* becomes subject to the *raṅga* (nasalization) when it occurs at the beginning of a pāda in a vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*). Example: *e*; *gabhīra ām̐ ugraputre*.

In *nadīṣvām̐ uśantam*, [the *ām*] follows *mitrayoḥ*; in *mitrayorām̐ eti*, [the *ām*] follows *asmadām̐ ṛcaḥ*; in *namasyurām̐ asṛkṣi*, [the *ām*] follows *carṣaṇīrām̐ aryaḥ*; in *īvadām̐ adevaḥ*, [the *ām*] follows *carṣaṇibhya ām̐ āviḥ*; in *joṣamām̐ indraḥ*. Why "at the beginning of a *pāda*"? [Observe: *somaṃ vajriṇa ābharat*. Why "after these" (*ebhyaḥ*)? [Observe: *sthūrayorādhvan*. Why "uncombined" (*apṛktam*)? [Observe: *mahitvaikam*. [The example] *gautama iti*: the word *iti* excludes the requirement that it be at the beginning of a *pāda*.

In the passage beginning with *upa prayanta* and including *imaṃ stomam* in the middle, the final syllable of the word *aminanta* becomes *raṅga* (nasalized) when followed by a word beginning with a vowel. Example: *ā te suparṇā aminanta evaiḥ*. What about in the *Gautama* school? When followed by a consonant (*aci*)? This must be considered. It should be understood that this applies everywhere in *saṃhitā*. In the *Agnitrimaṇḍala*: from *abodhyagniṃ* up to, but not including, *tvaṃ hyagne*, the final syllable of the word *eva* becomes *raṅga* when followed by the word *agni*. Example: *evām̐ agniṃ vasūyavaḥ*. What about in the *Atrimaṇḍala*? As in: *evāgniṃ sahasyam*. || 36,37 ||
The mother who is most excellent, the all-pervading, the sustainer, the praiseworthy—through fear of her, Parucchepa, the seer, [spoke] on the path toward the highest, primordial sound. 38.

Regarding *ṛpare* (before an *ṛ*-vowel): the finals of the six words beginning with *yā* become *raṅga* when followed by an *ṛ*-vowel. *Yā*: *paritakmyāyām ṛṇaṃ ca ye*; *kadām ṛtacit*; *mātām ṛṇuta*; *vibhvām ṛbhuḥ*; *vidhartām ṛtam*; *vipanyām ṛtasya*. Why "before an *ṛ*-vowel"? [Observe: *uta vibhyānu*. Regarding *bhīṣa*: in the passage from "agnim hotāram" up to "vediṣade," the finals of the words *bhīṣā* and *pathā* become *raṅga* when followed by the vowel *a*. *Bhīṣām adrivaḥ*; *pathām anehasā*. Why [is this restricted to] Parucchepa? [Observe: *mahaspasthātikrāme*. Why "in the first syllable"? [Observe: *patheva yantau*. || 38 ||

Wherever the elision of the letter *r*, the *uṣman* sounds, or the nasal (*n*) is observed, there the preceding vowel also undergoes the change to *mām̐s-p-*, *mām̐ś-c-*, or *am̐ś-c-* [respectively]. (39)

*Repheti*: When a *n* at the end of a word preceded by a long vowel undergoes the change to *r*, elision (*lopa*), or becomes a spirant (*ūṣman*), the preceding vowel becomes nasalized (*raṅga*). Examples: *ut paṇīrhataṃ*; *bandhūṃ ri mām*; *sargāmiva*; *dadhanvāṃ yaḥ*; *svavāṃ yātu*; *vidvāṃścikitvān*; *yāśco nu*; *māṃspacanyāḥ*; *māṃśca tve*; *maṃścatorvaruṇasya*. This specific rule for each case is intended to prevent nasalization (*raṅga*) in instances such as *cakṣūṃṣīva*. (39)
The tremulous (*kampa*) and the colored (*raṅga*) [notes] depend on the vowels; they follow the short and long [vowels].
Just as a coward finds a long [time], the rules for the long vowel apply to the protracted (*pluta*). 40.

In the verse of Medhātithi, there are three protracted vowels (*pluta*) in "adhaḥsvidāsīt upariḥsvidāsīt," occurring at the end of the *varuṇānta* and *vratānta* sections before a following semivowel (*yaṇ*).
In the case of touch as well, their [names] are short; likewise, we are Mitrā and Aparā.
You two are the physicians of the Āditya gods and of the Asuras belonging to Varuṇa.
The domestic priest worships Supratīka with power and sovereignty;
he who is born from a long throat [chants] thus at the Ṛkāra in the steps where the rite is perfected. || 43 ||

Regarding "svara" (accent): because they depend on vowels, the *kampa* and *raṅga* accents are short when the vowel is short, and long when the vowel is long. Examples: *kva3vośvāḥ*; *kvā3bhīśavaḥ*; *evām̐ agniṃ vasūyavaḥ*; *kadām̐ ṛtacit*. He speaks of the *pluta* (protracted) vowels: "of a short [vowel]" (*hrasvasya*). Whether at the end of a foot or in the middle of a word, that lengthening which occurs in the *saṃhitā* during the time of recitation for a short vowel is called *pluta*. Examples: *makṣūmakṣū kṛṇuhi*; *nū martaḥ*.

Alternatively, because these *pluta* vowels are numerous, irregular, and included within the category of "long" (*dīrgha*), only those *pluta*s that will be mentioned [in the following rules] are intended here. For example: *na tvā bhīriva vindatī 3*, *adhasvidāsī3duparisvidāsī3t*. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). In this *saṃhitā*, there are exactly three *pluta*s. He states the short vowel: *medhā*.

Beginning from "agniṃ dūtam" up to before "kasya nūnam," when the words ending in the term *varuṇāvrata* occur, there is a short vowel in *saṃhitā* before a *yaṇ* (semivowel), a *yaralava* (any consonant except *ha*), or a *sparśa* (stop) follows. Examples: *indrā varuṇa nūnu*, *indrāvaruṇa yām*, *dhṛtavratamitrāvaruṇa dūlabham*. Why [is this] not so in the case of Medhātithi? [Because it says: *indrāvaruṇā made*, *indrāvaruṇā yuvam*. Why [must it be] followed by a *sparśa* or a *yaṇ*? [Because in: *tā mitrāvaruṇā huve*. Likewise: when the word *mitra* occurs, there is a short vowel before the word *vayam* follows.

"We and the wise patrons [are] friends. Who are "we"? Those two, Mitra and Varuṇa. Regarding the word *ādityā*: whether followed by any one of the eight words beginning with *purohiti*—namely *ādityā*, *devā*, *varuṇā*, or *asurā*—the vowel becomes short. Alternatively, [it means] "O God, you heal" (*deva bhiṣajyathaḥ*). "This divine priesthood" (*iyaṃ deva purohitiḥ*). "O Varuṇa, of beautiful countenance" (*varuṇa supratīkam*). "The Āditya through power" (*ya āditya śavasā*). "O Varuṇa, the dominion" (*varuṇa kṣatram*). "O Varuṇa, he who offers" (*varuṇa dāśati*). "O Asura, we have come" (*asura yāmahi*). "O God, the place of atonement" (*deva niṣkṛtam*). In these cases, what [is the rule]? [It applies to] *indrāvaruṇā yuvam*.

"Thus": when an *ṛ* follows a word ending in the vowel *ā*, the *ā* becomes short. This rule is for the purpose of preventing the suspicion of a short vowel in cases such as *agna indraḥ* and *vāya ukthebhiḥ*. (40–43)

Since the characteristics are infinite, he states that these must necessarily be known: "Generally, even the qualities of accents, measures, places of articulation, and phonemes must be explained by those who know the sequence of phonemes; this has been elucidated here in brief."
Composed by the scholar who has bowed at the lotus feet of the master who has reached the further shore of the Vedas, for the delight of the wise. || 44 ||
Thus ends the definition of the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) according to the *Ṛgveda*.

Regarding the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*): although those who know the sequence of phonemes [know] the accents such as the acute (*udātta*), the measures (*mātrā*) such as the short (*hrasva*), and—by the force of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)—the articulations of the phonemes such as firmness and laxity, the points of articulation such as the throat, and the qualities of the phonemes such as contact (*spṛṣṭa*), slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*), openness (*vivṛta*), slight openness (*īṣadvivṛta*), closure (*saṃvṛta*), expansion (*vivāra*), contraction (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), and the qualities of being voiced with little breath (*alpaprāṇa*) or great breath (*mahāprāṇa*); furthermore, by the force of the word "also" (*api*), they should also know the stops (*sparśa*), semivowels (*antaḥstha*), sibilants (*ūṣman*), and the properties of being aspirated (*soṣman*), unaspirated (*aghoṣa*), and so on, as well as the [social] castes (*varṇa*) such as Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.

Nevertheless, because they are numerous, it was stated that what has been mentioned must necessarily be known; thus, the definition has been stated in brief. He concludes with the word "veda. || 44 ||
Thus the commentary is completed.
